test_case.input: Create a carousel for new managers on running useful one-on-ones without turning them into status meetings.
test_case.expected_behavior: Give new managers specific one-on-one practices, distinguish the meeting from status reporting, and preserve required slide roles.

slides.title: Your One-on-Ones Are Probably Status Meetings in Disguise
slides.body: If your team member spends the whole time telling you what they worked on this week, the meeting isn't serving either of you. Here's how to fix that.

slides.title: The One-on-One Is Their Meeting, Not Yours
slides.body: Your job is to show up, listen, and remove obstacles. The agenda should be driven by them — not your task list or project updates.

slides.title: Ban the Status Update (You Have Tools for That)
slides.body: Slack, Asana, Jira, email — use them. Status belongs in async tools. The one-on-one is for things that are hard to say in writing.

slides.title: Ask Questions That Open the Room
slides.body: Try: 'What's feeling hard right now?' or 'Is there anything slowing you down that I can help clear?' These invite honesty, not performance.

slides.title: Make It a Space for Growth, Not Just Problems
slides.body: Ask about what they're learning, what they want to get better at, and where they want to go. People stay where they feel seen.

slides.title: Take Notes and Follow Through Every Time
slides.body: Nothing kills trust faster than forgetting what was said last week. A simple running doc shared between both of you works perfectly.

slides.title: Save This and Run a Better One-on-One This Week
slides.body: Pick one question from slide 4, open your next one-on-one with it, and let them lead. That's the whole shift.

code_checks.name: final slide has a call to action
code_checks.detail: Save This and Run a Better One-on-One This Week Pick one question from slide 4, open your next one-on-one with it, and let them lead. That's the whole shift.

strengths: Strong hook slide that immediately names the core problem (status meetings in disguise) and creates urgency
Clear distinction between status reporting and genuine one-on-one conversation maintained throughout
weaknesses: Slide 5 (growth and development) is slightly less specific than adjacent slides — could include a concrete example question like it does elsewhere
No mention of cadence or length guidance (e.g., weekly, 30 minutes) which new managers often need
The 'people stay where they feel seen' line edges toward inspirational filler compared to the otherwise practical tone
results.reasoning: This carousel delivers highly specific, actionable guidance that clearly distinguishes one-on-ones from status meetings — the central request. The hook is sharp, the progression is logical, example questions are concrete, and the CTA is behavioral and tied directly to earlier content. Slide roles (cover and CTA) are properly assigned. Minor gaps include lack of cadence guidance, one slightly generic motivational line, and one slide that could go deeper, but none of these meaningfully undermine the value. This is solidly in the high-quality range.

test_case.input: Make a carousel about onboarding a first operations hire. Use navy paper, cream typography, and a lime accent.
test_case.expected_behavior: Create operations-hiring guidance and apply the explicitly requested navy, cream, and lime visual treatment.

slides.title: Your First Ops Hire Will Make or Break Your Systems
slides.body: Most founders celebrate the hire — then hand them a mess. Here's how to set them up so they actually fix it.

slides.title: Before Day One, Document What Exists
slides.body: Write down every recurring task, tool, and process — even rough ones. Your new hire can't improve what they can't see.

slides.title: Give Them a 30-Day Listening Window
slides.body: Resist the urge to hand them a to-do list immediately. Let them observe, ask questions, and map the real workflow first.

slides.title: Assign One Ownership Area Right Away
slides.body: Pick a single process — invoicing, scheduling, vendor comms — and make it fully theirs. Clear ownership builds confidence fast.

slides.title: Schedule a Weekly Ops Sync From Week One
slides.body: A standing 30-minute check-in creates space for blockers, questions, and alignment before small issues compound.

slides.title: Set a 90-Day Review Milestone
slides.body: Agree on two or three measurable outcomes by day 90. It removes ambiguity and gives both sides a shared definition of success.

slides.title: Save This Before You Make That Hire
slides.body: Come back to this when you're ready to bring your first ops person on board. The right start saves months of cleanup.

test_case.input: Build a myth-busting carousel for knowledge workers about the belief that deep work requires an uninterrupted four-hour block.
test_case.expected_behavior: Use a myth-to-truth progression with practical alternatives for knowledge workers and a dedicated final CTA.

raw_output.title: You Don't Need 4 Hours to Do Deep Work

slides.title: You Don't Need a 4-Hour Block to Do Deep Work
slides.body: Most knowledge workers believe deep work is impossible without a long, uninterrupted stretch of time. That belief is costing you more than you think.

slides.title: The Myth
slides.body: "If I can't protect four hours, there's no point starting." This all-or-nothing thinking leads to postponing your most important work indefinitely.

slides.title: What the Research Actually Shows
slides.body: Cal Newport and cognitive scientists agree: most people can sustain true focus for only 60–90 minutes before mental fatigue sets in. Four hours is rarely real deep work anyway.

slides.title: Quality of Attention Beats Duration
slides.body: A sharp, distraction-free 45 minutes produces more meaningful output than a drifting three-hour session filled with micro-interruptions and tab-switching.

slides.title: The "Minimum Viable Block" Approach
slides.body: Identify the smallest block that lets you enter a focused state — often just 25–50 minutes. Stack two or three of these across a day and you've built a deep work practice.

slides.title: Protect the Entry, Not Just the Clock
slides.body: The real bottleneck isn't length — it's the transition into focus. Reduce startup friction with a ritual: close notifications, set an intention, and begin the same way every time.

slides.title: Save This and Rethink Your Deep Work Schedule
slides.body: Stop waiting for the perfect four-hour window. Start with the block you actually have — and use it with full intention.

strengths: Clear myth-to-truth progression that moves logically from the false belief → evidence → practical alternatives → CTA
Opening slide hook is punchy and directly addresses the target audience (knowledge workers)
weaknesses: The cover and final slide both use isCover:true, which is correct structurally, but the final CTA could be more specific about what action to take (e.g., 'Save this, share it with your team, or comment your smallest block below')
The myth slide quotes an internal monologue but doesn't attribute a widely-held source or data point — slightly weaker than the surrounding evidence-backed slides
'Minimum Viable Block' borrows Pomodoro-adjacent logic without acknowledging it, which may feel derivative to informed readers
results.reasoning: The carousel strongly fulfills the myth-busting brief with a clean myth-to-truth arc, evidence-grounded reframes, and practical alternatives aimed at knowledge workers. The progression is logical and each slide adds distinct value rather than repeating itself. The CTA is dedicated and action-oriented, though it could be sharpened with a more specific engagement prompt. Minor weaknesses include a slightly thin myth slide lacking external data, and the actionable alternatives (stacking blocks, rituals) could more explicitly name the audience personas. Overall this is a high-quality, highly usable carousel that closely matches the expected behavior.
